title: Asking an AI tool good questions
essentialQuestion: How can you get a useful answer from an AI tool, and how do you know if it is right?
learningGoal: Improve a prompt for an AI tool by making it specific, and check the tool's answer against a trusted source.

rows: AI is a kind of technology. It is used in many places. Some people like it and some people do not.

sections.heading: An AI chat tool guesses its answers
sections.text: Some AI tools answer questions in writing, almost like a person in a chat. These tools are called chatbots. A chatbot learned from enormous amounts of writing, and it answers by guessing which words are likely to come next. Its answers can sound friendly, clever and completely certain. But a chatbot does not understand the world the way you do, so its guesses can be wrong. This lesson uses a pretend tool called the Hillview homework helper. Its answers were written in advance, so you can practise safely without the internet.
sections.simpler: Some AI tools answer questions in writing. They are called chatbots. A chatbot learned from lots and lots of writing. It tries to guess which words come next. Its answers can sound friendly and very sure. But it does not understand things like you do. So its guess can be wrong. This lesson uses a pretend tool. It is called the Hillview homework helper. Its answers are written already. So you can practise with no internet.

sections.heading: Clear prompts get better answers
sections.text: The question or instruction you give a chatbot is called a prompt. A vague prompt, like “Tell me about AI”, usually gets a vague answer. A specific prompt gets a more useful one. To make a prompt specific, say exactly what you want to know, who the answer is for and how long it should be. Compare “Tell me about AI” with “In two short sentences, explain what training data is, for a 12-year-old”. The second prompt gives the tool much more to work with. If the first answer isn't quite right, you can add another instruction, such as “Use an example about plants.”
sections.simpler: The question you give a chatbot is called a prompt. A vague prompt gets a vague answer. A specific prompt gets a better answer. Say what you want to know. Say who the answer is for. Say how long it should be. “Tell me about AI” is vague. “Explain training data for a 12-year-old” is specific. Not happy with the answer? Add more, like “Use an example about plants.”

sections.heading: Always check the answer
sections.text: Chatbots sometimes give answers that are wrong or completely made up. This is often called a hallucination. The difficult part is that a wrong answer can sound just as certain as a right one. When asked how many legs a spider has, the Hillview helper said six, “just like all insects”. The Hillview science book says spiders have eight legs and are not insects. So check important answers with a trusted source, such as a book, a teacher or an expert. Never type private information into a chatbot. For anything about health or safety, ask a person who knows.
sections.simpler: Chatbots sometimes give wrong answers. Some answers are made up. This is called a hallucination. A wrong answer can sound very sure. The Hillview helper said a spider has six legs. The science book says eight. Spiders are not insects. So check answers with a trusted source. A book, a teacher or an expert can help. Never type private information into a chatbot. For health or safety, ask a person.

glossary.definition: A computer program you can chat with in writing.
glossary.example: The Hillview homework helper is a pretend chatbot.

glossary.definition: The question or instruction you give an AI tool.
glossary.example: “Tell me about AI” is a vague prompt.
A vague prompt gets a vague answer.

glossary.definition: Clear and exact, with the details that matter.
glossary.example: A specific prompt says what you want, who it is for and how long.

glossary.definition: A wrong or made-up answer from an AI tool that sounds real.
glossary.example: “Every spider has six legs” is a hallucination.

glossary.definition: A person, book or place that is known to give correct information.
glossary.example: The Hillview science book is a trusted source.

write.prompt: Write a specific prompt for the Hillview helper about a topic from this course. Then explain how you would check its answer.
sentenceStarters: To make it specific, I added ...
To check the answer, I would ...
I would not type ___ into a chatbot because ...
selfCheck: I wrote a prompt that says what, who it is for and how long.
I explained what I added to make it specific.
I said how I would check the answer.
write.example: My first prompt was “Tell me about scams”. It was vague. To make it specific, I added what I want to know, who it is for and how long the answer should be. My new prompt is “In three short sentences, explain the warning signs of a scam, for a 12-year-old”. To check the answer, I would compare it with Lesson 6. I would also ask a teacher. I would not type a full name or address into a chatbot. That is private information.

speak.partnerTask: Say a vague prompt. Your partner makes it specific by adding what, who it is for, or how long. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud two ways to make a prompt better, and one way to check an answer.

watch.title: What are AI Chatbots?
watch.why: This short cartoon explains why many chatbots are made to sound like people.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why do you think a chatbot can sound like a real person?
watch.afterQuestion: Why should you check what a chatbot says, even when it sounds sure?
watch.summary: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing, a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains that many chatbots are made to sound human. They can sound friendly and very sure of themselves. They may agree with you, ask you questions as if they care, or act as if they know you. These things can make a chatbot feel like a friend. They can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person, and it can be wrong. So think about how a chatbot makes you feel, and stay in charge when you use one.
keyPoints: Many chatbots are made to sound like a person.
Sounding friendly and sure does not make an answer true.
Stay in charge: notice how a chatbot makes you feel, and check its answers.
watch.contentNote: An American cartoon for secondary school, about 3 minutes 20 seconds. The summary was written from Common Sense Education's description of the video and the lessons that use it, not from watching it, so check the summary before use. sensitiveNotes: Don't ask learners to type questions into a real AI tool in class, or to say what they have asked one. UNESCO's 2023 guidance recommends a minimum age of 13 for generative AI tools in the classroom, and many learners are younger. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline and safe.
educatorNotes: The tool's wrong answer about spiders is written on purpose, so learners practise checking (spiders have eight legs; insects have six). The explanation of chatbots (“guesses which words are likely to come next”) is a simplification; the AI-accuracy reviewer should check it.

Open question for reviewers (spec section 8, item 6): is a pretend tool with pre-written answers enough, or should a later version use an on-device model? Paper version of the activity: read the prompts and answers aloud and let learners choose.
